html:
Spoken, not really; written, quite possibly.

In writing, Dutch sits somewhere between English and German. Look at the Dutch numbers from one to ten: one moment they look like English, the next like German. It’s a dizzying, sunstroke-in-the-dark kind of confusion, and I honestly can’t tell which is which. If you know English and German, you can get the gist of most Dutch. For example, where English has an “ai” sound, Dutch writes ij; -ion becomes -ie (information → informatie); English help becomes Dutch helpen; English successful becomes Dutch succesvol (the Dutch pronounce the English v with a strong hint of f); a single e in German becomes a double e in Dutch (Bibliothek → bibliotheek); German Bestellung becomes Dutch bestelling (an order); and so on.

In pronunciation, Dutch is stubborn and has lots of sounds of its own: g is pronounced like a kind of h, ui sounds like you’re about to throw up, and there are loads of tongue-curling sounds. German is great in this respect. What you see is what you get: learn the basic vowels and consonants, and you can pronounce almost any word you see correctly, with few exceptions. English is a pain. Its pronunciation often defies logic, though at least it has no particularly weird sounds, or sounds that Mandarin speakers can’t make.

I’ve never actually studied Dutch; everything I know I picked up just from living here.
